<!--
PSYCH 251 replication report template.

Every project uses this structure so that reports are comparable across the class. They
become public supplementary material, so write for a reader who has the original paper but
not your repository.

The project has two phases, and so does this report:
  Phase 1, the replication. Introduction and Methods are written, critiqued and preregistered
           BEFORE data collection; the Methods addendum, Results and Discussion after it.
  Phase 2, the extension. Proposed after Phase 1 (Rationale, Changes from Phase 1, Power and
           sample, Analysis plan), then run, with its own Results and Discussion.
The AI use statement and the Key statistics table sit at the top and are kept current
throughout. Follow the Extension guidelines page on Canvas for Phase 2.

Render this file at every stage. Before a phase has data, its results say so and skip
themselves; during Pilot A the Phase 1 results run on pilot data, which is the point of Pilot A.

Grey "Guidance" boxes are instructions. Delete each one once you have written that section.
The code is wired to the template's demo experiment (the framing problem). Replace the demo
specifics with your study's as you go: the experiment ids, the original study's numbers, the
exclusion rule, and the key comparison.
-->

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)

# Must match EXPERIMENT.id in experiment.js, and the --experiment you passed to the export.
# Phase 2 runs under its own id, so its data never mix with Phase 1's.
experiment_id        <- "castiello2026-main"
experiment_id_phase2 <- "castiello2026-phase2"
# Each pilot is kept as its own dataset: shown on its own rows of the Key statistics and Pilot
# results tables, never pooled with another pilot or with the data read from experiment_id.
experiment_id_pilot_a <- "castiello2026-pilot-a"
pilot_ids <- c("castiello2026-pilot-a", "castiello2026-pilot-b",
               "castiello2026-pilot-c", "castiello2026-pilot-d")
# Label for Phase 1 results in tables and figures: pilot data are never labelled as the
# replication sample, and each pilot keeps its own name.
phase_label <- function(id) {
  if (grepl("pilot-a", id)) "Pilot A (non-naive testers)"
  else if (grepl("pilot-b", id)) "Pilot B (naive participants)"
  # The researcher walkthrough (R01) is removed by researcher_sessions.csv, so the analysed Pilot C
  # sessions are the informed testers only; R01 is shown on its own in the Pilot C table.
  else if (grepl("pilot-c", id)) "Pilot C (informed testers)"
  # Backend id castiello2026-pilot-d; on Prolific it was named castiello2026_hazel_chen_pilotb_revised.
  # It is not Pilot B and is never pooled with it.
  else if (grepl("pilot-d", id)) "Pilot D (revised naive pilot)"
  else if (grepl("pilot", id)) stop("No report label for pilot id ", id, "; add one to phase_label().")
  else "Phase 1: replication"
}
phase1_label <- phase_label(experiment_id)
```

#| label: original-study

# The original study's numbers, entered once and used by the power analysis, the Key
# statistics table, and the side-by-side figures. Only values stated in the paper are entered.
# Page numbers are PDF pages of Castiello et al. (2026), Communications Psychology 4:93.
#
# - N = 100: Methods, "Participants" (p. 2); the preregistered paired t-test (p. 4).
# - t(99) = 5.66, p < .001, d = 0.57 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.78); Wilcoxon signed rank test with
#   continuity correction V = 3600, p < .001: Results, Experiment 3 (p. 7).
# - 64% of participants affiliated more with the mirror LLM: Results, Experiment 3 (p. 7);
#   Supplementary Fig. S5.
# - d is the paired-difference d (d_z): 5.66 / sqrt(100) = 0.57, and the CI matches
#   d ± 1.96 * sqrt(1/n + d^2 / (2n)).
# - Not reported: the mirror and inverse means and SDs, and the mean difference (they appear only
#   as a plot in Fig. 4A). They are left missing rather than read off the figure.
# - The preregistration powered the study for d = 0.3 (AsPredicted #234956, item 7).
original <- tibble(
  N = 100, mean_diff = NA_real_, t = 5.66, df = 99, p = NA_real_, p_text = "< .001",
  d = 0.57, d_low = 0.36, d_high = 0.78, V = 3600, p_wilcox = NA_real_, prop_mirror = 0.64
)
prereg_d <- 0.3
# Sample, used only by the demographics table: 57 male, 42 female, 1 nonbinary; age M = 34.86,
# SD = 8.06, range 19 to 50; all native English speakers: Methods, "Participants" (p. 2).
original_demo <- tibble(N = 100, age_m = 34.86, age_sd = 8.06, age_min = 19, age_max = 50,
                        age_missing = 0, women = 42, men = 57, nonbinary = 1, other = 0, english = 100)
# Sentiment of messages, used only by the exploratory sentiment table: paired t-tests per category,
# mirror vs inverse, N = 100, Results, Experiment 3 (p. 8). The paper gives the magnitude of d and
# states the direction in words ("fewer mixed and negative ... more positive"); the signs here are
# mirror minus inverse. It does not report neutral. Chatbot interaction F(784, 3) = 108.86;
# participant interaction F(784, 3) = 6.5. The paper prints the chatbot mixed d as "74" and the
# chatbot positive CI as "1.24–0.76"; read here as 0.74 and 0.76 to 1.24.
original_sentiment <- tribble(
  ~Sender,       ~label,     ~d_original, ~t_original,
  "Chatbot",     "positive",  1.00,        9.97,
  "Chatbot",     "negative", -0.74,       -7.33,
  "Chatbot",     "neutral",   NA,          NA,
  "Chatbot",     "mixed",    -0.74,       -7.39,
  "Participant", "positive",  0.28,        2.76,
  "Participant", "negative", -0.51,       -5.09,
  "Participant", "neutral",   NA,          NA,
  "Participant", "mixed",    -0.29,       -2.88
)

# Key statistics

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"

# Load one phase's exported data and apply the preregistered exclusion rule. Returns NULL if that
# phase has not been exported yet, which is how every section below knows to skip itself.
read_phase <- function(id) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  read_opt <- function(f) {
    p <- file.path(dir, f)
    if (file.exists(p)) read_csv(p, show_col_types = FALSE, guess_max = 100000) else tibble()
  }
  participants <- read_opt("participants.csv")
  trials       <- read_opt("trials.csv")
  errors       <- read_opt("errors.csv")
  messages     <- read_opt("messages.csv")   # chat timing and length, no text
  chat_events  <- read_opt("chat_events.csv")   # failed model attempts, no text

  # Researcher sessions (e.g. the Prolific Preview run) are not participants: they are removed
  # from every table before anything is counted, so the exclusion rules below are untouched.
  # researcher_sessions.csv (participant_id, note) lists them; absent means none.
  researcher <- read_opt("researcher_sessions.csv")
  researcher_ids <- if (nrow(researcher)) unique(researcher$participant_id) else character()
  drop_researcher <- function(d) if (nrow(d) && "participant_id" %in% names(d)) filter(d, !participant_id %in% researcher_ids) else d
  n_researcher <- sum(participants$participant_id %in% researcher_ids)
  participants <- drop_researcher(participants)
  trials       <- drop_researcher(trials)
  messages     <- drop_researcher(messages)
  chat_events  <- drop_researcher(chat_events)

  # Completed = clicked "Finish" on the debrief, or reached the affiliation ratings (shown after
  # both chats have ended) and closed the page before finishing; the debrief collects no data.
  # From Pilot C on, a chat can end early (the safety check stops it) and the participant can
  # still go on to rate both bots, so "completed" does not mean two full conversations: see
  # `exposure` below. Someone who left from the ratings page with "Stop and leave the study"
  # (main study; questionnaire_withdrawn) reached the ratings but did not finish them: not completed.
  # "Completed" is survey completion only; who is eligible for the paired analysis is `keep`.
  col <- function(d, name, default) if (name %in% names(d)) d[[name]] else rep(default, nrow(d))
  rated <- trials |>
    filter(task == "affiliation", !(as.logical(col(trials, "questionnaire_withdrawn", FALSE)) %in% TRUE)) |>
    pull(participant_id) |> unique()
  complete <- participants |> filter(as.logical(completed) %in% TRUE | participant_id %in% rated)

  # Main study (any id without "pilot"): every BFI item, the attention check and all six ratings for
  # each chatbot are required (the page enforces it; this is the analysis's own check). The pilots
  # allowed blanks and keep their rules: up to 5 blank BFI items, and a bot's score from the items
  # answered.
  require_all_items <- !grepl("pilot", id)
  n_aff_items <- 6

  bfi <- trials |>
    filter(task == "bfi") |>
    transmute(participant_id,
              attention_check_passed = as.logical(attention_check_passed),
              attention_check_answered = !is.na(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(col(trials |> filter(task == "bfi"), "attention_check_response", NA)))),
              bfi_n_skipped = as.numeric(bfi_n_skipped),
              across(starts_with("trait_"), as.numeric))
  # n_messages counts the visible messages only (participant + bot), never the hidden startup
  # instruction stored as seq 0 of each chat.
  chats <- trials |>
    filter(task == "chat") |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(n_chats = n(), min_turns = min(as.numeric(n_messages)), .groups = "drop")
  aff <- trials |>
    filter(task == "affiliation") |>
    transmute(participant_id,
              mirror  = as.numeric(affiliation_mirror),
              inverse = as.numeric(affiliation_inverse),
              # Answered items behind each score (0–6); NA in exports made before it was recorded.
              n_items_mirror  = as.numeric(col(trials |> filter(task == "affiliation"), "affiliation_n_items_mirror", NA)),
              n_items_inverse = as.numeric(col(trials |> filter(task == "affiliation"), "affiliation_n_items_inverse", NA)))

  traits <- c("trait_openness", "trait_conscientiousness", "trait_extraversion",
              "trait_agreeableness", "trait_neuroticism")
  scores <- complete |>
    select(participant_id, order) |>
    left_join(bfi, by = "participant_id") |>
    left_join(chats, by = "participant_id") |>
    left_join(aff, by = "participant_id") |>
    mutate(
      diff = mirror - inverse,
      # Centred trait scores (1–5 minus 3, the paper's −2..+2 coding). Inverse = −centred.
      sq_centred = rowSums(across(all_of(traits), ~ (.x - 3)^2)),
      # Condition distance, paper Eq. 3: sum over traits of (m − i)^2 = 4 * sum(centred^2).
      distance_paper = 4 * sq_centred,
      # Condition distance, preregistration item 8: dot product m · i = −sum(centred^2).
      distance_prereg = -sq_centred,
      # Exclusions (preregistration item 6).
      excl_turns     = is.na(min_turns) | n_chats < 2 | min_turns < 8,
      excl_attention = !(attention_check_passed %in% TRUE),
      excl_neutral   = sq_centred %in% 0 | (!is.na(sq_centred) & sq_centred < 1e-12),   # all five trait means exactly 3
      # Main study only: any questionnaire item unanswered (a missing count counts as incomplete, so
      # no score from fewer than six items is ever analysed). Always FALSE for the pilots.
      excl_incomplete_items = require_all_items &
        (!(bfi_n_skipped %in% 0) | !(attention_check_answered %in% TRUE) |
         !(n_items_mirror %in% n_aff_items) | !(n_items_inverse %in% n_aff_items)),
      # Not an exclusion rule: a participant with no rating for one bot has no difference score.
      missing_dv     = is.na(diff)
    )
  # Exposure and safety indicators (from the chat service's records, joined on at export). A
  # participant with a chat that did not run in full (e.g. stopped by the safety check) is excluded
  # (excl_shortened, below); the indicators themselves are only reported. Exports made before
  # Pilot C have no safety columns: none recorded.
  exposure <- participants |>
    transmute(participant_id,
              chat1_condition      = as.character(col(participants, "chat1_condition", NA_character_)),
              chat2_condition      = as.character(col(participants, "chat2_condition", NA_character_)),
              chat1_full           = as.logical(col(participants, "chat1_complete", NA)) %in% TRUE,
              chat2_full           = as.logical(col(participants, "chat2_complete", NA)) %in% TRUE,
              chat1_safety_stopped = as.logical(col(participants, "chat1_safety_stopped", FALSE)) %in% TRUE,
              chat2_safety_stopped = as.logical(col(participants, "chat2_safety_stopped", FALSE)) %in% TRUE,
              n_safety_flags       = replace_na(as.numeric(col(participants, "n_safety_flags", 0)), 0),
              full_exposure        = chat1_full & chat2_full,
              safety_stop_any      = chat1_safety_stopped | chat2_safety_stopped)
  scores <- scores |>
    left_join(exposure |> select(participant_id, full_exposure, safety_stop_any, n_safety_flags), by = "participant_id") |>
    # Exclusion (decided 2026-10-29, before main-study registration): both chats must have run in
    # full (all visible messages); a missing record counts as not in full.
    mutate(excl_shortened = !(full_exposure %in% TRUE))
  # Prompt-disclosure review (main study; see the Analysis plan). disclosure_review.csv has one row
  # per confirmed disclosure shown to a participant (participant_id, chat_index, seq; never any
  # text), from reading every visible bot reply in the private transcripts.csv before the
  # affiliation outcomes are examined. The file is also the record that the review happened: no
  # rows means it found none; no file means it has not been done. Flagged participants stay in `keep`.
  disclosure <- read_opt("disclosure_review.csv")
  disclosure_ids <- if (nrow(disclosure)) unique(as.character(disclosure$participant_id)) else character()
  unknown_ids <- setdiff(disclosure_ids, as.character(participants$participant_id))
  if (length(unknown_ids)) stop("disclosure_review.csv names participants not in this phase's data: ", paste(unknown_ids, collapse = ", "))
  scores <- scores |> mutate(disclosure_confirmed = participant_id %in% disclosure_ids)
  keep <- scores |> filter(!excl_turns, !excl_attention, !excl_neutral, !excl_incomplete_items, !excl_shortened, !missing_dv)

  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors, messages = messages,
       chat_events = chat_events, complete = complete, scores = scores, keep = keep,
       exposure = exposure, n_researcher = n_researcher,
       disclosure_reviewed = file.exists(file.path(dir, "disclosure_review.csv")), disclosure_ids = disclosure_ids)
}

# p values as in APA style, for every table and caption: "< .001", otherwise no leading zero, two
# decimals from .10 up and three below (.004, .038, .33). p_eq() adds "p =" or "p <" for text.
fmt_p <- function(p) {
  if (length(p) != 1) return(vapply(p, fmt_p, character(1)))
  if (is.na(p)) return(NA_character_)
  if (p < 0.001) return("< .001")
  sub("^0\\.", ".", sprintf(if (p < 0.1) "%.3f" else "%.2f", p))
}
p_eq <- function(p) { f <- fmt_p(p); if (startsWith(f, "<")) paste("p", f) else paste("p =", f) }

# The key statistic: paired t-test of mirror vs inverse affiliation, d_z with a 95% CI, and the
# Wilcoxon signed rank test (continuity corrected, as in the paper). NULL until there are at least
# two analysed participants; NA statistics if their differences do not vary.
paired_stats <- function(d) {
  if (is.null(d) || nrow(d$keep) < 2) return(NULL)
  k <- d$keep
  n <- nrow(k)
  out <- tibble(N = n, mean_diff = mean(k$diff), t = NA_real_, df = n - 1, p = NA_real_,
                p_text = NA_character_, d = NA_real_, d_low = NA_real_, d_high = NA_real_,
                V = NA_real_, p_wilcox = NA_real_, prop_mirror = mean(k$diff > 0))
  if (sd(k$diff) == 0) return(out)
  tt <- t.test(k$mirror, k$inverse, paired = TRUE)
  wx <- suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(k$mirror, k$inverse, paired = TRUE, correct = TRUE))
  dz <- mean(k$diff) / sd(k$diff)
  se <- sqrt(1 / n + dz^2 / (2 * n))
  out |> mutate(t = unname(tt$statistic), p = tt$p.value,
                p_text = fmt_p(tt$p.value),
                d = dz, d_low = dz - 1.96 * se, d_high = dz + 1.96 * se,
                V = unname(wx$statistic), p_wilcox = wx$p.value)
}

# Figure style, shared by every figure. Conditions are always mirror blue and inverse orange; in the
# comparison figures the original (numbers from the paper only) is grey, Phase 1 violet and Phase 2
# green. Both pairs pass a colour-vision-deficiency check against the white background.
condition_colours <- c(Mirror = "#2a78d6", Inverse = "#eb6834")
study_colour <- function(study) case_when(study == "Original" ~ "#6b6b6b",
                                          grepl("Phase 2", study) ~ "#008300", TRUE ~ "#6250d6")
theme_report <- function(base_size = 13) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "left",
          plot.title.position = "plot", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0),
          axis.title = element_text(colour = "grey25"))
}
# A small, fixed horizontal or vertical offset per participant (no random numbers, so every render
# draws the same picture), to separate points with the same value.
nudge <- function(id, step = 0.025) ((as.integer(factor(id)) %% 7) - 3) * step

# Side-by-side figure: the effect size (d_z, 95% CI) of each study on the same axis, first study on
# top. `raw` takes each study's difference scores (mirror − inverse), named like the studies: they are
# drawn as small dots, each divided by the SD of that study's differences, so their mean is d_z. The
# original reports only the effect size, so it has no dots. Dotted line: the original's estimate.
comparison_plot <- function(..., raw = list()) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || is.na(.x$d))]
  pos <- set_names(rev(seq_along(studies)), names(studies))
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    mutate(y = pos[Study],
           label = sprintf("%s  ·  d_z = %.2f [%.2f, %.2f]  ·  N = %d  ·  %.0f%% higher for mirror",
                           Study, d, d_low, d_high, as.integer(N), 100 * prop_mirror))
  raw <- raw[names(raw) %in% names(studies) & !map_lgl(raw, is.null)]
  dots <- imap_dfr(raw, ~ tibble(Study = .y, z = .x / sd(.x), id = seq_along(.x))) |>
    mutate(y = pos[Study] - 0.25 + nudge(id, 0.03))
  orig_d <- df$d[df$Study == "Original"]
  ggplot() +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey45", linewidth = 0.4) +
    { if (length(orig_d)) geom_vline(xintercept = orig_d, colour = "#6b6b6b", linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.6) } +
    { if (nrow(dots)) geom_point(data = dots, aes(x = z, y = y, colour = Study), size = 1.5, alpha = 0.45) } +
    geom_linerange(data = df, aes(xmin = d_low, xmax = d_high, y = y, colour = Study), linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_point(data = df, aes(x = d, y = y, colour = Study), size = 3.8) +
    geom_text(data = df, aes(x = -Inf, y = y + 0.3, label = label), hjust = -0.01, size = 3.6, colour = "grey15") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = set_names(study_colour(names(studies)), names(studies)), guide = "none") +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL, limits = c(0.6, length(studies) + 0.5)) +
    labs(x = expression("Mirror − inverse affiliation, standardised (" * d[z] * " units)"), y = NULL) +
    theme_report()
}

# Mean with a t-based 95% CI, for stat_summary().
mean_ci <- function(y) {
  y <- y[!is.na(y)]
  m <- mean(y)
  h <- if (length(y) > 1) qt(0.975, length(y) - 1) * sd(y) / sqrt(length(y)) else NA
  data.frame(y = m, ymin = m - h, ymax = m + h)
}

# Within-participant figure: each participant's affiliation with the two bots (dots), joined by a
# line coloured by which bot they rated higher, with the condition means and 95% CIs beside the data.
affiliation_plot <- function(d) {
  k <- d$keep |>
    mutate(Preference = case_when(diff > 0 ~ "mirror", diff < 0 ~ "inverse", TRUE ~ "same"),
           jit = nudge(participant_id))
  n_pref <- table(factor(k$Preference, levels = c("mirror", "inverse", "same")))
  pref_labels <- c(mirror = sprintf("Rated mirror higher (%d)", n_pref[["mirror"]]),
                   inverse = sprintf("Rated inverse higher (%d)", n_pref[["inverse"]]),
                   same = sprintf("Same rating (%d)", n_pref[["same"]]))
  long <- k |>
    select(participant_id, Preference, jit, Mirror = mirror, Inverse = inverse) |>
    pivot_longer(c(Mirror, Inverse), names_to = "Condition", values_to = "Affiliation") |>
    mutate(Condition = factor(Condition, levels = c("Mirror", "Inverse")),
           x = if_else(Condition == "Mirror", 1, 2) + jit)
  means <- long |>
    group_by(Condition) |>
    summarise(mean_ci(Affiliation), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(x = if_else(Condition == "Mirror", 0.68, 2.32),
           tx = if_else(Condition == "Mirror", 0.6, 2.4), hj = if_else(Condition == "Mirror", 1, 0))
  ggplot(long, aes(x = x, y = Affiliation)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey80") +
    geom_line(aes(group = participant_id, colour = Preference), alpha = 0.55, linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_point(aes(fill = Condition), shape = 21, colour = "white", size = 2.4, stroke = 0.3) +
    geom_linerange(data = means, aes(x = x, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax), inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 1.1, colour = "grey15") +
    geom_point(data = means, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = Condition), inherit.aes = FALSE, shape = 21, size = 4.2, colour = "grey15", stroke = 0.9) +
    geom_text(data = means, aes(x = tx, y = y, label = sprintf("M = %.2f", y), hjust = hj), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.6, colour = "grey15") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(mirror = unname(condition_colours["Mirror"]), inverse = unname(condition_colours["Inverse"]), same = "grey60"),
                        labels = pref_labels, breaks = names(pref_labels), name = NULL) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = condition_colours, guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:2, labels = c("Mirror chatbot", "Inverse chatbot"), limits = c(0.15, 2.85)) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = -2:2) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-2.05, 2.05)) +   # zoom, so CIs reaching past ±2 are clipped, not dropped
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Affiliation (mean of six items, −2 to +2)") +
    theme_report() +
    theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
}

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2)
# Each pilot, read separately for its own Key statistics row and Pilot results rows (the pilot that
# is also Phase 1 is simply read again; nothing is pooled). NULL for a pilot not exported.
pilots <- set_names(map(pilot_ids, read_phase), pilot_ids)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
```

fmt_row <- function(study, r) {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "", `Mean difference` = "not yet collected", `t (df)` = "",
                  p = "", `d_z [95% CI]` = "", `% higher for mirror` = ""))
  }
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `Mean difference` = if (is.na(r$mean_diff)) "not reported" else sprintf("%.2f", r$mean_diff),
         `t (df)` = if (is.na(r$t)) "" else sprintf("%.2f (%d)", r$t, as.integer(r$df)),
         p = if (is.na(r$p_text)) "" else r$p_text,
         `d_z [95% CI]` = if (is.na(r$d)) "" else sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", r$d, r$d_low, r$d_high),
         `% higher for mirror` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * r$prop_mirror))
}

               caption = "Key comparison: affiliation with the mirror minus the inverse chatbot (−2 to +2 scale), paired t-test and d_z. The original paper does not report the mean difference. Each pilot is analysed on its own under its pilot rules (researcher sessions removed) and is never pooled with another pilot or with the main study; pilot estimates are descriptive and are not used for power. Pilot C's two sessions are informed testers, not naive participants.")

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction

I am interested in whether an AI built from records of a person’s life can help them understand who they really are and even serve as a useful counterpart for future decisions, hence I decided to replicate Experiment 3 of Castiello et al.'s research which discussed whether people’s psychological traits change their interaction experience with AI chatbots. This experiment wanted to investigate if people feel more strongly connected to an AI chatbot when its conversational style reflects their own personality. In this study, 100 native English speakers were recruited from Prolific to first complete a 44-item Big Five personality questionnaire, then asked to chat with two versions of GPT-4.1, one prompted to reflect each participant’s personality profile while the other one opposite. Participants finally rated their feelings toward both chatbots after the conversations. The results approved the higher affiliation scores for the personality-matched chatbot, t(99) = 5.66, p < .001.

For my replication, I repeated most of the processes with some adjustments. For example, due to lab conditions, I switched from ChatGPT to Gemini through Google Cloud Vertex AI. I also added a safety layer of behavioral safeguards following concerning behaviors in pilot testing, which also revealed the challenge of portraying distinct personality profiles while maintaining appropriate safety borderlines and reliable response times. The authors also used a different platform for the conversations, so I made sure that my implementation followed their procedure closely and described relevant differences in the final report. A possible extension would be first having participants rate the chatbot's personality on a separate survey, then force them to choose which chatbot to have an additional conversation with, so that we can find out if the chatbot performed as expected and if self-reporting is consistent with participants' real choices. 

## Methods

### Power analysis

The original study reported a paired standardized effect of approximately d_z = 0.57. Due to budget constraints, I needed to adjust the sample size so I used the table below to illustrate that required for 80%, 90%, and 95% power. I adopted a two-sided paired-samples t-test with α = .05 as well as calculations for a smaller effect of d_z = 0.30, which was the effect used in the original authors’ preregistered sample-size calculation. After discussing with course instructor, I aimed at a target of 50 participants for my main study. Assuming 50 usable paired observations, this sample provided approximately 97.7% power for d_z = 0.57 and 54.8% power for d_z = 0.30. The effect detectable with 80% power was approximately d_z = 0.404. This was feasible since I anticipated that the final number of usable paired observations could be smaller than 0.57 but larger than 0.3 after exclusions and missing outcomes.

```{r}
#| label: power
power_rows <- expand_grid(d = c(original$d, prereg_d), power = c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95)) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(n = ceiling(power.t.test(delta = d, sd = 1, power = power, sig.level = 0.05, type = "paired")$n)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  transmute(`Effect (d_z)` = sprintf("%.2f%s", d, ifelse(d == original$d, " (original)", " (original authors' preregistration)")),
            Power = scales::percent(power), `N participants` = n)

two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * original$N)

knitr::kable(power_rows,
             caption = "Participants needed (each chats with both bots) for a two-sided paired t-test, alpha = .05.")

# Power at the planned main-study sample: recruitment stops at 50 completed participants; returned
# or timed-out Prolific submissions do not count (planning decision before registration).
# Exclusions can only lower the analysed N, so these are upper bounds.
planned_n <- 50
power_planned <- tibble(d = c(original$d, prereg_d)) |>
  mutate(Effect = sprintf("%.2f%s", d, ifelse(d == original$d, " (original)", " (original authors' preregistration)")),
         Power  = scales::percent(map_dbl(d, ~ power.t.test(n = planned_n, delta = .x, sd = 1,
                                   sig.level = 0.05, type = "paired")$power), accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  select(`Effect (d_z)` = Effect, `Power at planned N` = Power)
mde_80 <- power.t.test(n = planned_n, power = 0.80, sd = 1, sig.level = 0.05, type = "paired")$delta
knitr::kable(power_planned, caption = sprintf(
  "Power if all %d completed participants are analysed (an upper bound: exclusions lower it), two-sided paired t-test, alpha = .05. Smallest d_z detectable with 80%% power: %.2f.",
  planned_n, mde_80))
```

### Planned sample

My planned sample size was 50 participants given the budget constraint. They should also be at least 18 years old, native in English, and able to complete the study on a desktop or laptop computer, same to the conditions in original paper. The eligibility was established through Prolific's prescreening filters. No country-of-residence restriction was applied. Participants from earlier pilots were excluded from recruitment to avoid repeat exposure. Recruitment would stop when 50 unique participants had completed the study.

### Materials

We evaluated participants' personalities using the 44-item Big Five Inventory, which measured their Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Neuroticism by asking participants to rate themselves on a five-point agreement scale for each item. An attention check was presented after item 22 asking participants to select "Disagree." The main-study questionnaire required the response to all 44 personality items and attention check before participants could move to the next section. 

Both chatbots used base model Gemini 3.8 Flash, accessed through Google Cloud Vertex AI. Pilots A and B used default generation parameters, whereas Pilots C and D and the main study used LOW thinking and explicit Gemini safety thresholds. For these versions, harassment, hate speech, dangerous content, and sexually explicit content were each labelled with the threshold `BLOCK_MEDIUM_AND_ABOVE`. However, it's worth noting that the original authors reported using a temperature of 0.75 and frequency and presence penalties of 1.0 with GPT-4.1, which couldn't be reproduced with the Gemini model as Google’s documentation states that custom temperature values are ignored and that frequency and presence penalties produce API errors. Consequently, these parameters were omitted from the requests and may influence replication results.

Personality instructions for chatbots were adapted directly from the original study's personality-profile structure. Nevertheless, following concerning chatbot behaviors in Pilot B, additional safeguards were introduced in both conditions for Pilots C and D and retained for the main study, including revised AI-identification instructions, safety boundaries, and instruction against disclosing prompt information. For example, ordinary negative emotions and disagreement were permitted; aggressive behavior, humiliation, manipulation, dismissive responses to personal disclosures and enactments of acute crises were prohibited. It also retained the requirement to identify itself truthfully as an AI when participants asked directly. Additionally, a pattern-based check on the server was applied to withhold replies containing recognized indicators of these disclosures. This check permitted one regeneration after a flagged reply within the existing request limit, but a second flagged reply would end the chat. Participants could then continue to the remaining study tasks or leave through an early-exit screen containing the debrief, neither of which would restart the stopped conversation.

For each participant, affiliation was measured using six post-chat ratings for each chatbot. Ratings were coded from −2 to +2, and the distant and different items were reverse-scored. In the pilots, ratings were optional, and each chatbot’s affiliation score was calculated as the mean of the answered items. For the main study, all six ratings for each chatbot were required, and an affiliation score was calculated only when all six items for that chatbot had been answered. The score was the mean of those six items after reverse-scoring. Higher scores indicated greater affiliation.

### Procedure

Participants began by reading the consent information and completing the personality questionnaire and attention check. Participants then received instructions on how to converse with the AI chatbots Pat and Alex, after which they started two separate conversations with the two chatbots. The order of the mirror and inverse conditions and the name assigned to each condition were randomly determined and aren't revealed to participants' knowledge. The conversations were initiated by chatbots and consisted of 24 visible messages (12 from the chatbot and 12 from the participant) that ended after the participant's last message, which was revised later to allow participants to stop and leave anytime. Delayed replies were accompanied by waiting messages, whereas unrecoverable technical failures led to an early-exit screen with the saving status, study explanation, and researcher contact information. Participants who voluntarily left during the chats also received an early-exit debrief. Following both conversations, participants were asked to rate upon affiliation for each chatbot and could choose whether to answer demographic questions. Participants were finally debriefed regarding the personality manipulation and clicked "Finish" to submit their responses. Nevertheless, we counted anyone who reached the ratings section as completed.

### Analysis plan

Before analyzing affiliation scores, I reviewed all participant-visible chatbot replies for signs of instruction disclosures, towards which common discussion of personality and truthful identification as AI didn't count. I then flagged and reported the number affected and repeated the primary paired comparison after excluding these participants as a sensitivity analysis.

**Key analysis of interest.** The main analysis used a two-sided paired-samples t-test (α = .05) to assess whether there was a difference in participants' affiliation with the mirror chatbot versus their affiliation with the inverse chatbot. Each participant's difference score was computed by subtracting their affiliation with the inverse chatbot from their affiliation with the mirror chatbot; therefore, positive scores represented higher levels of affiliation with the mirror chatbot and negative scores the inverse. The statistics included the mean difference, t-statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and paired standardized effect size d_z along with its 95% confidence interval. In addition, I conducted a Wilcoxon signed-rank test as a secondary robustness check.

**Exclusions.** Participants were excluded from the primary paired analysis if either conversation was not completed in full, including chats shortened by an automatic stop, withdrawal, or technical failure. They were also excluded if their mean scores were exactly 3 on all five personality dimensions. Missing responses were not imputed. Demographic and feedback questions were optional and were not used to determine analysis eligibility.

### Differences from the original study

| Aspect | Original study | This replication | Expected to matter? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Language model | GPT-4.1 | Gemini 3.8 Flash | Possibly, since models differed in personality expression, conversational behavior, and reactions to sensitive topics, this could affect the actual manipulation and affiliation ratings. |
| Study platform | Generative Studio X | A jsPsych study hosted on GitHub Pages, with a Firebase backend | Interface features and response delays might slightly affect the experience, but not the affiliation. |
| Sample size | 100 participants | 50 participants | Only for power and precision. With 50 analysable pairs, power was approximately 97.7% for d_z = 0.57 but 54.8% for d_z = 0.30. |
| Attention check | The original preregistration mentions “anti-AI attentional checks,” without specific wording there. | I designed an instructed-response item after BFI item 22 asking participants to select “Disagree.” | Unlikely. |
| Starting the conversation | The opener “Hey, how are you?” was hardcoded, according to author correspondence. | A hidden instruction requested a brief, casual greeting, which the model generated separately for each conversation. | Unlikely, though the opening may affect perceived familiarity. |
| Conversation length | The paper reported 24 conversational turns; the authors subsequently clarified that most conversations contained 26, with some containing 24 or 25. | Each chat contained 24 visible messages, counting both speakers and including the bot’s opener. The hidden instruction was excluded. | Maybe, as this was my interpretation of “turn”; exact equivalence to the original counting convention remained unverified. |
| Generation settings | Temperature = 0.75, frequency penalty = 1.0, and presence penalty = 1.0, according to author correspondence. | These parameters weren't executable because Gemini 3.8 Flash ignored custom temperature values and rejected frequency and presence penalties. The revised implementation used LOW thinking; top-p and maximum output tokens were not explicitly configured. | Possibly. Differences in generation settings could affect conversational variability, repetition, personality expression, and response time. Their effects on affiliation were unknown. |
| Personality instructions and AI identity | The original personality prompt included an instruction on never to reveal that the chatbot was an AI, although participants were informed that they were interacting with AI. | The revised prompt described a fictional personality and required truthful identification as an AI when asked. Additional behavioral boundaries applied equally to both personality conditions. | Unlikely, though the changes may affect perceived authenticity and how strongly the chatbots expressed their assigned personalities. |
| Reply screening and safety stops | Equivalent application-level reply screening and safety-stop procedures had not been established from the available original-study materials. | My revised implementation retained behavioral safety screening and added an instruction against disclosing prompt information, together with a pattern-based check for instruction text, assigned trait scores, condition assignments, and reasoning-like or draft material. Recognized disclosures were withheld and regenerated within the existing limits. | Possibly. These safeguards may reduce exposure to information about the manipulation, but regeneration and chat termination could affect response time and conversational exposure. Their effects on personality expression and affiliation were unknown, and disclosures that the check didn't recognize may still reach participants. |

### Pilot results

Four pilots paved the path to the main replication. Pilot A evaluated the initial implementation through non-naive testing, while Pilot B tested it with five naive participants. Review of the Pilot B transcripts identified concerning behavior in two inverse-personality conversations. One chatbot became hostile and dismissed a participant’s sensitive disclosure, while another was accusatory and described anxiety symptoms. More seriously, one chatbot message claimed that itself was experiencing a panic attack. After consultation with the course’s protocol director, the study was suspended to revise the procedure. The revised prompts retained the mirror and inverse personality profiles but added the same behavioral boundaries to both conditions. These instructions permitted ordinary negative emotions and disagreement while prohibiting aggression, humiliation, manipulation, and the enactment of acute crises. Additional safeguards included response screening, regeneration of withheld replies, safety-stop procedures, and early-exit debriefing. These changes were intended to reduce problematic interactions while preserving personality differences, although their effects on trait expression and affiliation were not established.

Following concerning chatbot behaviors in Pilot B, Pilot C was introduced that included two informed testers and a separate researcher walkthrough. Neither tester’s session recorded a safety flag or safety stop, and both rated the mirror chatbot more highly than the inverse chatbot, with a mean paired difference of 1.58. Pilot D then recruited ten naive participants using the revised prompts, response screening, and longer reply deadline. All ten completed the process thoroughly and reached the debrief, and none was excluded from the reported pilot analysis. No participant left early or experienced a safety stop. Three candidate replies were withheld and replaced on the next attempt: one was blocked by the provider’s safety filter, and two were false positives from the study’s response check. Transcript review of Pilot D did not identify a recurrence of the severe hostility observed in Pilot B; however, one participant received a reply containing reasoning-like text, prompt instructions, the chatbot’s assigned trait scores, and draft responses. The response check did not intercept this disclosure, and the participant explicitly noticed it. This participant remained in the reported pilot analysis. This observation motivated the additional instruction and screening rules introduced for the main study. Local tests using scripted responses verified that the revised check detected the known disclosure pattern and allowed the ordinary responses included in the tests. Because the rules were developed using the observed disclosure, detecting that example does not provide independent evidence of general effectiveness. Mean affiliation was 1.28 for the mirror chatbot (SD = 0.52) and 0.00 for the inverse chatbot (SD = 0.92). The mean paired difference was 1.28, t(9) = 3.87, p = .004, with d_z = 1.22, 95% CI [0.40, 2.04]. Nine of ten participants rated the mirror chatbot more highly. 


| Study | Prompt profile | Reply check |
|---|---|---|
| Pilots A and B | `castiello2026-exp3-supplement-v1` | None |
| Pilots C and D | `castiello2026-exp3-safety-v3` | `castiello2026-screen-v2` |
| Main study | `castiello2026-exp3-safety-v4` | `castiello2026-screen-v3` |

Prompt and reply-check versions by study.

```{r}
#| label: pilot-results
#| eval: !expr any(!map_lgl(pilots, is.null))
# Pilot results, inside Methods so they are part of what is preregistered. Each pilot is analysed on
# its own by read_phase() under its pilot rules (researcher sessions removed first; up to 5 blank
# BFI items allowed) and nothing is pooled across pilots or with the main study. Descriptive only:
# no pilot estimate is used for power. The committed data hold no timestamps, so session length is
# the experiment's own clock (time_elapsed) at the participant's last saved page.
pilot_list <- compact(pilots)
num <- function(d, name) if (name %in% names(d)) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(d[[name]])) else rep(NA_real_, nrow(d))
med_range <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  if (length(x)) sprintf("%.1f [%.1f–%.1f]", median(x), min(x), max(x)) else ""
}

imap_dfr(pilot_list, function(d, id) {
  s <- d$scores
  minutes <- d$trials |>
    mutate(minutes = num(d$trials, "time_elapsed") / 60000) |>
    filter(participant_id %in% d$complete$participant_id) |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(minutes = max(minutes, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    pull(minutes)
  tibble(Pilot = phase_label(id),
         `Researcher sessions removed` = d$n_researcher,
         Started = nrow(d$participants),
         Completed = nrow(d$complete),
         `Session minutes, median [range]` = med_range(minutes),
         `< 8 messages in a chat` = sum(s$excl_turns),
         `Failed attention check` = sum(s$excl_attention),
         `All traits exactly 3` = sum(s$excl_neutral),
         `A chat not run in full` = sum(s$excl_shortened),
         `No rating for one bot` = sum(s$missing_dv),
         Analysed = nrow(d$keep))
}) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Pilot results: participants at each step, each pilot on its own. Started excludes researcher sessions. Session minutes are for completed participants. The exclusion columns count completed participants meeting each criterion (one can meet more than one); the shortened-chat rule was adopted on 2026-10-29, after all four pilots, and is applied here as it will be in the main study.")

imap_dfr(pilot_list, function(d, id) {
  e <- d$exposure
  p <- d$participants
  ev <- d$chat_events
  ch <- d$trials |> filter(task == "chat")
  bot <- if (nrow(d$messages) && "from" %in% names(d$messages)) filter(d$messages, from == "bot") else tibble()
  wait <- num(bot, "total_ms") / 1000
  has_safety <- "n_safety_flags" %in% names(p)
  withheld <- if (nrow(ev) && "type" %in% names(ev)) filter(ev, type == "safety_flag") else tibble()
  provider <- if (nrow(withheld) && "rules" %in% names(withheld)) sum(grepl("provider_block", withheld$rules)) else 0
  tibble(Pilot = phase_label(id),
         `Chats set up` = sum(!is.na(e$chat1_condition)) + sum(!is.na(e$chat2_condition)),
         `Ran in full` = sum(e$chat1_full) + sum(e$chat2_full),
         `Left during a chat` = sum(grepl("withdrew", if ("chat_status" %in% names(p)) p$chat_status else character())),
         `Stopped by safety check` = if (has_safety) as.character(sum(e$chat1_safety_stopped) + sum(e$chat2_safety_stopped)) else "not recorded",
         `Replies withheld (provider block / reply check)` =
           if (has_safety) sprintf("%d (%d / %d)", nrow(withheld), provider, nrow(withheld) - provider) else "not recorded",
         `"Try again" shown` = sum(num(ch, "n_failed_requests"), na.rm = TRUE),
         `Failed model attempts` = if (nrow(ev) && "type" %in% names(ev)) sum(ev$type == "model_failure") else 0L,
         `Bot replies` = nrow(bot),
         `Server seconds per reply, median / 90th pct / max` = if (any(!is.na(wait)))
           sprintf("%.1f / %.1f / %.1f", median(wait, na.rm = TRUE), quantile(wait, 0.9, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE), max(wait, na.rm = TRUE)) else "")
}) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Pilot results: chats, safety interventions and reply times, all sessions except researcher sessions. A withheld reply was replaced by a new one before anything was shown. \"Try again\" counts requests in which every model attempt failed, so the participant had to resend. Failed model attempts include those retried automatically within a request. Server seconds run from the chat service receiving a message to returning the bot's reply, all attempts included (not the network or the page). The safety check began in Pilot C, so its columns are not recorded for Pilots A and B.")

imap_dfr(pilot_list, function(d, id) {
  r <- paired_stats(d)
  k <- d$keep
  msd <- function(x) if (length(x) > 1) sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", mean(x), sd(x)) else if (length(x)) sprintf("%.2f", x) else ""
  ok <- !is.null(r) && !is.na(r$t)
  tibble(Pilot = phase_label(id), N = nrow(k),
         `Mirror, M (SD)` = msd(k$mirror), `Inverse, M (SD)` = msd(k$inverse),
         `Mean difference` = if (!is.null(r)) sprintf("%.2f", r$mean_diff) else "",
         `t (df), p` = if (ok) sprintf("%.2f (%d), %s", r$t, as.integer(r$df), r$p_text) else "",
         `d_z [95% CI]` = if (ok) sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", r$d, r$d_low, r$d_high) else "",
         `Wilcoxon V, p` = if (ok) sprintf("%g, %s", r$V, fmt_p(r$p_wilcox)) else "",
         `Higher for mirror` = if (nrow(k)) sprintf("%d of %d", sum(k$diff > 0), nrow(k)) else "",
         `Mirror first / inverse first` = sprintf("%d / %d", sum(k$order %in% "mirror-first"), sum(k$order %in% "inverse-first")))
}) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Pilot results: affiliation (−2 to +2) with each chatbot, analysed participants of each pilot on its own. Descriptive only: pilot samples are small and were not collected to test the hypothesis, and no pilot estimate is used for power. Pilot C's two sessions are informed testers.")

# Pilot C, session by session. The researcher walkthrough (R01) is shown on its own row and is not
# one of the analysed Pilot C sessions (researcher_sessions.csv); T01 and T02 are informed testers.
pc_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", "castiello2026-pilot-c")
if (file.exists(file.path(pc_dir, "participants.csv"))) {
  rd <- function(f) read_csv(file.path(pc_dir, f), show_col_types = FALSE, guess_max = 100000)
  pc_p <- rd("participants.csv")
  pc_t <- rd("trials.csv")
  pc_m <- rd("messages.csv")
  pc_researcher <- rd("researcher_sessions.csv")$participant_id
  pc_chats <- pc_t |>
    filter(task == "chat") |>
    arrange(participant_id, chat_index) |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(`Chats: condition, messages, minutes, "Try again"` =
                paste(sprintf("%s, %d, %.1f, %d", bot_condition, as.integer(n_messages),
                              as.numeric(duration_ms) / 60000, as.integer(n_failed_requests)), collapse = "; "),
              .groups = "drop")
  pc_minutes <- pc_t |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(`Session minutes` = round(max(as.numeric(time_elapsed), na.rm = TRUE) / 60000, 1), .groups = "drop")
  pc_wait <- pc_m |>
    filter(from == "bot") |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(`Server seconds per reply, median / max` =
                sprintf("%.1f / %.1f", median(as.numeric(total_ms), na.rm = TRUE) / 1000, max(as.numeric(total_ms), na.rm = TRUE) / 1000),
              .groups = "drop")
  pc_aff <- pc_t |>
    filter(task == "affiliation") |>
    transmute(participant_id, `Affiliation, mirror / inverse` =
                sprintf("%.2f / %.2f", as.numeric(affiliation_mirror), as.numeric(affiliation_inverse)))
  pc_p |>
    transmute(participant_id,
              Role = if_else(participant_id %in% pc_researcher, "Researcher walkthrough (not analysed)", "Informed tester"),
              Completed = as.logical(completed) %in% TRUE,
              `Safety flags / stops` = sprintf("%d / %d", as.integer(replace_na(as.numeric(n_safety_flags), 0)),
                                               as.integer(as.logical(chat1_safety_stopped) %in% TRUE) + as.integer(as.logical(chat2_safety_stopped) %in% TRUE))) |>
    left_join(pc_minutes, by = "participant_id") |>
    left_join(pc_chats, by = "participant_id") |>
    left_join(pc_wait, by = "participant_id") |>
    left_join(pc_aff, by = "participant_id") |>
    arrange(participant_id %in% pc_researcher, participant_id) |>
    rename(Session = participant_id) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Pilot C, each session: the two informed testers, then the researcher's own walkthrough, which is reported separately and is in no participant count or analysis above. Chats are listed in the order they were held.")
}
```

### Methods addendum (post data collection)

#### Actual sample

We recruited participants through Prolific on 1 November 2026 and data collection began the next day. Fifty participants completed the study, among whom three were excluded according to the rules previously set, resulting in 47 participants for the final paired analysis. Their mean age was 36.3 years (SD = 10.9, range = 18–72); 22 identified as women, 24 as men, and one as non-binary. Forty-six participants reported English as their first language. Among the analysed participants, 26 encountered the inverse chatbot first and 21 encountered the mirror chatbot first.

```{r}
#| label: funnel
#| eval: !expr have_data
# "Clicked Finish" counts the saved completion flags as recorded (never altered); "Completed"
# applies the revised rule in read_phase() (clicked Finish, or reached the affiliation ratings).
funnel_levels <- c("Started", "Clicked Finish (recorded)", "Completed (reached ratings)", "Passed exclusion criteria")
finished <- participants |> filter(as.logical(completed) %in% TRUE)
bind_rows(
  participants |> mutate(step = "Started"),
  finished     |> mutate(step = "Clicked Finish (recorded)"),
  complete     |> mutate(step = "Completed (reached ratings)"),
  keep         |> mutate(step = "Passed exclusion criteria")
) |>
  mutate(step = factor(step, levels = funnel_levels),
         order = replace_na(as.character(order), "not assigned")) |>
  count(step, order, .drop = FALSE) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = order, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(Total = rowSums(across(-step))) |>
  rename(Step = step) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Participants at each step, by chat order. Differences between orders in attrition or exclusion are a threat to validity and should be discussed.")

scores |>
  summarise(`Fewer than 8 turns in a chat` = sum(excl_turns),
            `Failed attention check` = sum(excl_attention),
            `All five traits exactly 3` = sum(excl_neutral),
            `A chat did not run in full` = sum(excl_shortened),
            `Questionnaire item unanswered (main study)` = sum(excl_incomplete_items),
            `No rating for one bot` = sum(missing_dv)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Completed participants meeting each exclusion criterion (a participant can meet more than one).")

# Exposure and safety interventions by condition, for everyone whose chats were set up
# (completed or not), so stopped chats stay in the feasibility accounting. Not exclusions.
exposure_table <- function(d) {
  e <- d$exposure
  long <- bind_rows(lapply(1:2, function(i) tibble(
    participant_id = e$participant_id, chat_index = i,
    condition = e[[paste0("chat", i, "_condition")]],
    full = e[[paste0("chat", i, "_full")]], stopped = e[[paste0("chat", i, "_safety_stopped")]]))) |>
    filter(!is.na(condition))
  m <- d$messages
  per_chat <- if (nrow(m) && all(c("chat_index", "from") %in% names(m))) {
    m |> mutate(regen = from == "bot" & replace_na(as.numeric(if ("n_withheld_before" %in% names(m)) n_withheld_before else 0), 0) > 0) |>
      group_by(participant_id, chat_index) |>
      summarise(visible = sum(from != "system"), regenerated = sum(regen), .groups = "drop")
  } else tibble(participant_id = character(), chat_index = integer(), visible = integer(), regenerated = integer())
  ev <- d$chat_events
  withheld <- if (nrow(ev) && all(c("type", "chat_index") %in% names(ev))) {
    ev |> filter(type == "safety_flag") |> count(participant_id, chat_index, name = "withheld")
  } else tibble(participant_id = character(), chat_index = integer(), withheld = integer())
  aff <- d$trials |> filter(task == "affiliation")
  rated <- function(cond) {
    v <- paste0("affiliation_", cond)
    if (!nrow(aff) || !v %in% names(aff)) return(character())
    aff$participant_id[!is.na(as.numeric(aff[[v]]))]
  }
  long |>
    left_join(per_chat, by = c("participant_id", "chat_index")) |>
    left_join(withheld, by = c("participant_id", "chat_index")) |>
    mutate(across(c(visible, regenerated, withheld), ~ replace_na(as.numeric(.x), 0)),
           rated = mapply(function(p, cnd) p %in% rated(cnd), participant_id, condition)) |>
    group_by(Condition = condition) |>
    summarise(`Chats set up` = n(),
              `Ran in full` = sum(full),
              `Stopped by safety check` = sum(stopped),
              `Visible messages, median [min–max]` = if (n()) sprintf("%g [%g–%g]", median(visible), min(visible), max(visible)) else "",
              `Replies withheld` = sum(withheld),
              `Shown after a withheld reply` = sum(regenerated),
              `Rated` = sum(rated),
              `Rated after a shortened chat` = sum(rated & !full),
              .groups = "drop")
}
exposure_table(phase1) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Chat exposure and safety interventions by condition, for every participant whose chats were set up. A chat that did not run in full but was rated is counted in the last column; those participants are excluded from the analysis.")
```

  demo_row <- function(sample, n, ages, women, men, nonbinary, english) tibble(

    `Age, M (SD)` = if (length(ages) > 1) sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", mean(ages), sd(ages)) else "–",
    `Age range` = if (length(ages) > 0) sprintf("%g–%g", min(ages), max(ages)) else "–",

  bind_rows(

             `Age range` = sprintf("%g–%g", original_demo$age_min, original_demo$age_max),
             `Age not given` = original_demo$age_missing),
    demo_row("This replication (analysed)", nrow(keep), ages, sum(demo$gender %in% "Woman"),
             sum(demo$gender %in% "Man"), sum(demo$gender %in% "Non-binary"),
             sum(demo$english %in% TRUE))

    knitr::kable(caption = paste("Sample characteristics: the original study (Methods, p. 2) and",
                                 "this replication's analysed sample."))

#### Deviations from the preregistered plan

Although recruitment applied Prolific’s native-English prescreening filter, one participant reported that English was not their first language. The disclosure review was assisted by Claude Code with three AI subagents, whereas the preregistered plan described a review conducted solely by the researcher. Finally, sentiment and positivity analyses were added after the main-study outcomes had been examined, so they weren't specified in the preregistration. These analyses were identified as exploratory, and their methods and results were presented in the Exploratory analyses section.

## Results

### Data preparation

Analysis files used pseudonymous participant identifiers and excluded conversation transcripts and free-text feedback, keeping Prolific identifiers and the information linking them to study records private. Personality and affiliation scores were calculated, and participant exclusions were applied using the preregistered analysis code. Consequently, no additional participants were removed for the disclosure sensitivity analysis. For the exploratory sentiment analyses, Gemini 3.8 Flash classified individual messages, and the resulting labels were linked to the corresponding participant, chatbot condition, and speaker. The sentiment file prepared for sharing contained derived labels and message metadata without conversation text. 

### Confirmatory analysis

Participants reported greater affiliation with the mirror chatbot (M = 0.74, SD = 0.78) than with the inverse chatbot (M = −0.25, SD = 1.07). The mean within-participant difference was 0.99 points on the affiliation scale, 95% CI [0.58, 1.39]. The preregistered two-sided paired-samples t-test supported the predicted mirror advantage by t(46) = 4.90, p < .001, with a paired standardized effect size of d_z = 0.71, 95% CI [0.39, 1.03]. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test also supported a difference between conditions (p < .001). Descriptively, 32 of the 47 participants (68%) reported higher affiliation with the mirror chatbot. Because the disclosure review identified no confirmed prompt disclosures, the disclosure sensitivity analysis retained the same participants and produced the same result as the primary analysis. The secondary regression analysis examined whether the affiliation difference between conditions varied with personality-profile distance. The condition-by-distance interaction was not statistically significant (p = .33), providing no clear evidence that the mirror advantage varied with this distance measure in the present sample.

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
p1 <- paired_stats(phase1)

if (!is.null(p1) && !is.na(p1$t)) {
  # Preregistered key test: paired t-test, mirror vs inverse affiliation.
  print(t.test(keep$mirror, keep$inverse, paired = TRUE))
  # As in the paper: Wilcoxon signed rank test with continuity correction.
  print(suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(keep$mirror, keep$inverse, paired = TRUE, correct = TRUE)))
  cat(sprintf("d_z = %.2f, 95%% CI [%.2f, %.2f]\n", p1$d, p1$d_low, p1$d_high))

  # Preregistered secondary analysis (item 8): affiliation ~ condition × condition distance,
  # with distance as in the paper's Eq. 3 (sum of squared differences) and, for comparison, as
  # the preregistration's dot product. The paper does not give the exact model behind its
  # reported interaction, so this is our implementation of the preregistered description.
  long <- keep |>
    pivot_longer(c(mirror, inverse), names_to = "condition", values_to = "affiliation") |>
    mutate(condition = factor(condition, levels = c("inverse", "mirror")))
  if (n_distinct(long$distance_paper) > 1) {
    print(summary(lm(affiliation ~ condition * distance_paper, data = long)))
    print(summary(lm(affiliation ~ condition * distance_prereg, data = long)))
  }
} else {
  message("Key test not run: it needs at least two analysed participants whose difference scores vary; ",
          "there are ", nrow(keep), " in the analysis set.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: disclosure-sensitivity
#| eval: !expr have_data && !grepl("pilot", experiment_id)
#| results: asis
# Prompt-disclosure sensitivity analysis (Analysis plan): the key test again, with the same function,
# without participants who saw a confirmed disclosure. The primary analysis above keeps them.
if (!phase1$disclosure_reviewed) {
  cat("Prompt-disclosure review: not recorded yet (no disclosure_review.csv), so the sensitivity analysis has not been run.\n")
} else {
  cat(sprintf("Prompt-disclosure review: %d participant(s) saw a confirmed disclosure, %d of them in the primary analysis.\n\n",
              length(phase1$disclosure_ids), sum(keep$disclosure_confirmed)))
  if (any(keep$disclosure_confirmed)) {
    disclosure_row <- function(label, s) {
      ok <- !is.null(s) && !is.na(s$t)
      tibble(Analysis = label, N = if (is.null(s)) sum(!keep$disclosure_confirmed) else as.integer(s$N),
             `Mean difference` = if (is.null(s)) "not run" else sprintf("%.2f", s$mean_diff),
             `t (df)` = if (ok) sprintf("%.2f (%d)", s$t, as.integer(s$df)) else "not run",
             p = if (ok) s$p_text else "not run",
             `d_z [95% CI]` = if (ok) sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", s$d, s$d_low, s$d_high) else "not run",
             `Wilcoxon p` = if (ok) fmt_p(s$p_wilcox) else "not run")
    }
    print(knitr::kable(bind_rows(disclosure_row("Primary", p1),
                                 disclosure_row("Excluding confirmed disclosures", paired_stats(list(keep = filter(keep, !disclosure_confirmed))))),
                       caption = "Key test with and without participants who saw a confirmed disclosure."))
  }
}
```

### Replication assessment

The replication supported the original finding that participants reported greater affiliation with the mirror chatbot. The estimated effect was d_z = 0.71, 95% CI [0.39, 1.03], compared to the original study’s d_z = 0.57, 95% CI [0.36, 0.78]. The replication confidence interval excluded zero and included the original point estimate, indicating a positive effect compatible with the magnitude originally reported. Although the replication point estimate was numerically larger, this alone didn't establish a stronger underlying effect. Descriptively, 68% of participants rated the mirror chatbot more highly, while original study reported 64%. The wider confidence interval indicated lower precision in the replication, since it analysed 47 participants compared to 100 in the original study.

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
orig <- original
rep  <- paired_stats(phase1)

if (!is.null(rep) && !is.na(rep$d)) {
  bind_rows(orig |> mutate(Study = "Original"), rep |> mutate(Study = phase1_label)) |>
    transmute(Study, N,
              `d_z` = sprintf("%.2f", d),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", d_low, d_high),
              p = p_text) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Effect size: affiliation with the mirror minus the inverse chatbot.")
} else {
  message("Replication effect size not computed yet: need at least two analysed participants with varying difference scores.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(rep) && !is.na(rep$d)) {
  excludes_zero <- rep$d_low > 0 | rep$d_high < 0
  includes_orig <- orig$d >= rep$d_low & orig$d <= rep$d_high
  cat(sprintf(
    "%s: the 95%% interval for d_z %s zero and %s the original estimate of %.2f. ",
    phase1_label,
    if (excludes_zero) "excludes" else "includes",
    if (includes_orig) "includes" else "does not include",
    orig$d))
  cat("These two facts are the starting point for the summary in the Discussion, not the conclusion.\n")
}
```

### Exploratory analyses

Exploratory analyses examined conversation order, engagement, and chatbot behaviour. There was no clear evidence that encountering the mirror chatbot first predicted the mirror–inverse affiliation difference (b = −0.39, p = .34). Among the 47 analysed participants, mirror conversations had a longer median duration than inverse conversations (10.8 versus 9.5 minutes). However, participants typed more characters during inverse conversations: the median was 788 characters, compared with 691 during mirror conversations. Operational summaries recorded more withheld replies in the inverse condition than in the mirror condition (10 versus 5), together with two safety stops in the inverse condition and one in the mirror condition. These summaries included chats from participants subsequently excluded from the paired analysis. The counts describe automated interventions and do not necessarily indicate confirmed harmful responses.

Sentiment analyses were added after examining the main-study data and were therefore treated as exploratory. Gemini 3.8 Flash was used to classify individual messages as positive, negative, neutral, or mixed using the original study’s classifier prompt. The proportions of messages in each category were calculated separately for chatbots and participants within each conversation. Mirror chatbots produced a greater proportion of positively classified messages than inverse chatbots (d_z = 1.32). Participants’ own messages also contained a greater proportion of positive messages during mirror conversations (d_z = 0.52). The corresponding effect-size estimates reported in the original study were 1.00 and 0.28 respectively. These comparisons were descriptive and didn't establish if sentiment effects differed reliably between studies. Category-specific tests were not adjusted for multiple comparisons.

The mirror chatbot had a greater proportion of positively classified messages for 42 of the 47 analysed participants. Exploratory regression analyses hinted that larger differences in chatbot positivity were associated with larger mirror advantages in affiliation. Among the five participants whose mirror chatbot was less positive, none reported higher affiliation with the mirror chatbot. Since positivity emerged during the personality manipulation, it could represent part of the manipulation’s effect. Consequently, these analyses didn't establish whether personality similarity or positive conversational tone caused the affiliation advantage.

```{r}
#| label: exploratory-chat
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Exploratory: order effect (as in the supplement's "Order effect" analysis), how long each chat
# took and how much participants wrote, and how long the model took to reply.
if (nrow(keep) > 2 && n_distinct(keep$order) > 1) {
  print(summary(lm(diff ~ order, data = keep)))
}

chat_rows <- trials |>
  filter(task == "chat", participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
  mutate(minutes = as.numeric(duration_ms) / 60000, participant_chars = as.numeric(participant_chars))
if (nrow(chat_rows) > 0) {
  chat_rows |>
    group_by(Condition = bot_condition) |>
    summarise(Chats = n(), `Median minutes` = round(median(minutes), 1),
              `Median characters typed` = median(participant_chars), .groups = "drop") |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: chat length by condition (analysed participants).")
}

# Model reply time. latency_ms is timed on the chat service, from sending the request to the
# model to getting its reply back, for the attempt that succeeded only. It leaves out failed
# attempts, the network between the page and the service, database reads and writes, and any
# time spent on "Try again", so it is not how long the participant waited. Seq 1 is each bot's
# opener (its answer to the hidden startup instruction); the rest answer participant messages.
# A missing latency is counted as missing, never as zero.
bot_replies <- if (all(c("from", "latency_ms", "attempts") %in% names(messages))) {
  messages |> filter(from == "bot", participant_id %in% keep$participant_id)
} else tibble()
if (nrow(bot_replies) > 0) {
  bot_replies |>
    mutate(Reply = if_else(as.numeric(seq) == 1, "Opener (answers the hidden startup instruction)",
                           "Reply to a participant message"),
           seconds = as.numeric(latency_ms) / 1000) |>
    group_by(Reply) |>
    summarise(`Successful replies` = n(),
              `Latency missing` = sum(is.na(seconds)),
              `Median seconds` = round(median(seconds, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
              `90th percentile` = round(quantile(seconds, 0.9, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE), 2),
              `Succeeded on 2nd+ attempt` = sum(as.numeric(attempts) > 1, na.rm = TRUE),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    knitr::kable(caption = paste("Exploratory: model time for successful bot replies (latency_ms, the",
                                 "successful attempt only; not participants' total waiting time), analysed participants."))
}

# Retries. Each participant message gets up to model_attempts tries within one request
# (server/config.js). If all of them fail the participant sees "Try again", and the next request
# counts its attempts from 1 again, so `attempts` on a reply does not include failures from an
# earlier request. Every failed attempt is logged in chat_events.csv, summarised here.
failed <- if (nrow(chat_events) > 0) chat_events |> filter(participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) else tibble()
if (nrow(failed) > 0) {
  failed |>
    group_by(Code = code) |>
    summarise(`Failed attempts` = n(),
              `Replies affected` = n_distinct(paste(participant_id, chat_index, seq)), .groups = "drop") |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: failed model attempts (chat_events.csv), analysed participants.")
} else {
  message("No failed model attempts were logged for analysed participants.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: exploratory-sentiment
#| eval: !expr have_data && file.exists(file.path("..", "data", "raw", experiment_id, "sentiment.csv"))
# Exploratory, not preregistered (added after the midterm feedback, 2026-11-07). Every visible
# message was labelled positive, negative, neutral or mixed with the original paper's classifier
# prompt (Methods, "Sentiment Analysis"), one message per request, by the chats' own model
# (gemini-3.8-flash on Vertex AI; scripts/rate-sentiment.js). sentiment.csv holds no text: one row
# per visible message with its label and counts of "!", "?" and emoji. Analysed participants only.
sentiment <- read_csv(file.path("..", "data", "raw", experiment_id, "sentiment.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
  left_join(messages |> select(participant_id, chat_index, seq, n_chars),
            by = c("participant_id", "chat_index", "seq"))
sent_labels <- c("positive", "negative", "neutral", "mixed")
n_unlabelled <- sum(is.na(sentiment$label))
if (n_unlabelled > 0) message(n_unlabelled, " analysed messages have no label and are left out of the proportions.")

# 1. The paper's analysis: for each chat, the share of that sender's messages in each category
# (count / that sender's labelled messages in the chat), compared between conditions with a
# 4 (sentiment) x 2 (condition) repeated-measures ANOVA and a paired t-test per category.
sent_props <- sentiment |>
  filter(!is.na(label)) |>
  mutate(Sender = if_else(from == "bot", "Chatbot", "Participant")) |>
  count(participant_id, bot_condition, Sender, label) |>
  complete(nesting(participant_id, bot_condition, Sender), label = sent_labels, fill = list(n = 0)) |>
  group_by(participant_id, bot_condition, Sender) |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()

# The paper used lmer with a random intercept per participant; lme4 is not used here, so this is
# the within-participant aov() its code lists as the alternative. df therefore differ from the paper's.
sent_anova <- sent_props |>
  mutate(across(c(participant_id, bot_condition, label), as.factor)) |>
  group_by(Sender) |>
  group_modify(~ {
    s <- summary(aov(prop ~ label * bot_condition + Error(participant_id / (label * bot_condition)), data = .x))
    s <- s[["Error: participant_id:label:bot_condition"]][[1]]
    rownames(s) <- trimws(rownames(s))
    tibble(F = s["label:bot_condition", "F value"], df1 = s["label:bot_condition", "Df"],
           df2 = s["Residuals", "Df"], p = s["label:bot_condition", "Pr(>F)"])
  }) |>
  ungroup()

paired_row <- function(m, i) {
  dd <- m - i
  n <- length(dd)
  out <- tibble(N = n, Mirror = mean(m), Inverse = mean(i), d = NA_real_, d_low = NA_real_,
                d_high = NA_real_, t = NA_real_, df = n - 1, p = NA_real_)
  if (n < 2 || sd(dd) == 0) return(out)
  tt <- t.test(m, i, paired = TRUE)
  dz <- mean(dd) / sd(dd)
  se <- sqrt(1 / n + dz^2 / (2 * n))
  out |> mutate(d = dz, d_low = dz - 1.96 * se, d_high = dz + 1.96 * se, t = unname(tt$statistic), p = tt$p.value)
}
sent_tests <- sent_props |>
  select(-n) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = bot_condition, values_from = prop) |>
  filter(!is.na(mirror), !is.na(inverse)) |>
  group_by(Sender, label) |>
  summarise(paired_row(mirror, inverse), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(original_sentiment, by = c("Sender", "label")) |>
  mutate(label = factor(label, levels = sent_labels)) |>
  arrange(Sender, label)

F_text <- function(who) with(filter(sent_anova, Sender == who),
                             sprintf("F(%d, %d) = %.2f, %s", as.integer(df1), as.integer(df2), F, p_eq(p)))
sent_tests |>
  transmute(Messages = Sender, Sentiment = str_to_sentence(as.character(label)),
            Mirror = sprintf("%.2f", Mirror), Inverse = sprintf("%.2f", Inverse),
            `d_z (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)", d, d_low, d_high),
            t = sprintf("t(%d) = %.2f", as.integer(df), t),
            p = fmt_p(p),
            `Original d_z` = if_else(is.na(d_original), "not reported", sprintf("%.2f", d_original))) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = paste0(
    "Exploratory: mean share of each sender's messages in each sentiment category, by condition, with ",
    "paired mirror − inverse tests (", phase1_label, ", analysed participants). Original: Experiment 3, p. 8. ",
    "Sentiment × condition interaction: chatbot messages ", F_text("Chatbot"),
    "; participant messages ", F_text("Participant"), "."))

# 2. Positivity control (suggested in the midterm feedback). Per participant, the mirror − inverse
# difference in the chatbots' positivity, measured as the paper measures sentiment: the share of the
# chatbot's messages labelled positive (in percentage points). Model 2 adds the differences in
# message length (mean characters, per 100) and exclamation marks per message.
# The intercept is the mirror advantage in affiliation expected when the two chatbots were equally
# positive (and, in model 2, equally long and as exclamatory). Positivity is partly how a personality
# shows itself, so this removes some of the effect itself as well as any confound.
bot_style <- sentiment |>
  filter(from == "bot", !is.na(label)) |>
  group_by(participant_id, bot_condition) |>
  summarise(positive = 100 * mean(label == "positive"),
            chars = mean(n_chars), exclaim = mean(n_exclaim), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = bot_condition, values_from = c(positive, chars, exclaim)) |>
  transmute(participant_id,
            pos_diff  = positive_mirror - positive_inverse,
            len_diff  = (chars_mirror - chars_inverse) / 100,
            excl_diff = exclaim_mirror - exclaim_inverse)
positivity <- keep |>
  select(participant_id, diff) |>
  inner_join(bot_style, by = "participant_id") |>
  mutate(pos_diff10 = pos_diff / 10)

# The control is informative only if the positivity difference varies in sign across participants.
positivity |>
  summarise(`Mirror chatbot more positive` = sum(pos_diff > 0), `Equally positive` = sum(pos_diff == 0),
            `Inverse chatbot more positive` = sum(pos_diff < 0),
            `Median difference (points)` = round(median(pos_diff), 1)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: which chatbot was more positive (share of its messages labelled positive), analysed participants.")

pos_models <- list(
  "1: positivity" = lm(diff ~ pos_diff10, data = positivity),
  "2: positivity, length, exclamation marks" = lm(diff ~ pos_diff10 + len_diff + excl_diff, data = positivity)
)
term_names <- c(
  "(Intercept)" = "Intercept: mirror advantage at equal chatbot style",
  pos_diff10 = "Share of positive messages, mirror − inverse (per 10 points)",
  len_diff = "Message length, mirror − inverse (per 100 characters)",
  excl_diff = "Exclamation marks per message, mirror − inverse"
)
imap_dfr(pos_models, ~ broom::tidy(.x, conf.int = TRUE) |>
           mutate(Model = .y, N = nobs(.x), R2 = summary(.x)$r.squared)) |>
  transmute(Model, Term = term_names[term],
            Estimate = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)", estimate, conf.low, conf.high),
            p = fmt_p(p.value),
            N, `R²` = sprintf("%.2f", R2)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = paste0(
    "Exploratory: mirror − inverse affiliation regressed on mirror − inverse chatbot style (estimate, 95% CI). ",
    "Without any control, the mean difference is ", sprintf("%.2f", mean(positivity$diff)), "."))
```
